item.title: Uncovering Multimorbidity Patterns Through a Novel Randomized Clustering Algorithm
item.description: arXiv:2611.26927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Patients with several chronic conditions rarely share the same combination: in four years of the nationally representative Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS), we find 32,789 distinct combinations of two to seven conditions, and over 90% of those involving four or more occur in a single patient. Methods that search for common combinations discard most of this heterogeneity. We present the Randomized Length Sequential Clustering Algorithm (RLSCA), which links diseases by lift, a pairwise association measure counted only above a user-set support threshold. A mixed-integer program repeatedly selects and removes the group of conditions with the greatest internal lift, up to a random size; 100 iterations yield a database of clusters scored by size, rediscovery frequency, and body systems spanned. In MEPS 2019, stratified by age and sex, RLSCA recovers known groupings at a high threshold, such as diabetes with lipid disorders and hypertension, and at a lower threshold returns clusters of up to eight conditions spanning five body systems. Frequent itemset mining, at its lowest feasible support, finds no set above five conditions; hierarchical clustering cannot control cluster size. With a clinical large language model, the database could suggest which further conditions a patient is at risk of.
item.dc:creator: Ali Jafari, Hari Balasubramanian

item.title: Beware of complexity bias: A hindrance to conceptual model generalization and interpretability
item.description: arXiv:2611.26995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the field of rainfall-runoff modeling, lumped conceptual models have been shown to be powerful representations of catchment filtering functions. They demonstrate fairly strong predictive performance in gauged catchments and have the ability to learn important intermediate latent variables and flow paths which increases their value as interpretable models. During calibration, these conceptual models may fit streamflow just as well as deep learning models, however, their performance often sharply degrades after deployment, suggesting the presence of overfitting. We hypothesize that complexity (or flexibility) bias is one of the causes of such overfitting. Complexity bias can appear within conceptual models when the number of effective degrees of freedom is parameter or flow path dependent. Using a popular conceptual model and a series of synthetic datasets, we illustrate the presence of complexity bias and demonstrate its impact on model interpretability/parameter inference. Then, using real rainfall-runoff data from CAMELS-US, we investigate if overfitting can be reduced by adding regularization terms that prevent complexity bias from forming. Our results suggest that conceptual and hybrid modeling can be further improved if hydrologists become aware of this pervasive bias.
item.dc:creator: Joseph Janssen, Yang Yang

item.title: Statistical and Machine Learning Approaches for Estimating Visitation to Natural Spaces in the UK
item.description: arXiv:2611.27668v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Natural spaces support health and well-being, but increasing recreational use can put pressure on ecologically sensitive sites. Understanding when, where and why people visit is important for planning, site management and evaluating interventions. Building on work by the Office for National Statistics, we developed statistical and machine learning models to predict visitor numbers at points located in natural spaces. We trained on automated people counter data across a range of green and blue spaces in England and Wales and tested the models' ability to generalise to unseen counter locations. Our models offer a scalable approach for predicting visitor numbers in natural spaces, reducing reliance on surveys and physical counters.
item.dc:creator: Yueyue Chai, Elizabeth Galloway, Peter Challenor, Pippa Langford

item.title: Synthetic Surrogate Functional Regression (SSFR): A Robust Framework for Estimating Spatially Varying Covariate Effects in Surrogate-Augmented Neuroimaging
item.description: arXiv:2611.27791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Relating demographic, clinical, and genetic covariates to high-dimensional imaging outcomes is a core problem in brain imaging, especially when the target modality is observed for only a subset of participants. Generative models can synthesize missing modalities from auxiliary data, but using synthetic images in regression requires care to ensure valid inference. We propose a two-stage Synthetic Surrogate Functional Regression (SSFR) framework for spatially varying covariate effects under partially observed imaging outcomes. By calibrating surrogate information against observed target images, SSFR improves efficiency while remaining robust to discrepancies between the surrogate and target regression functions. We establish consistency and the convergence rate of the estimator, and show that first-stage surrogate-model estimation error does not alter its asymptotic rate. We introduce a voxelwise surrogate explanatory measure $R^2(z)$, the fraction of residual target-image variation explained by a candidate surrogate; with the observation rate, it gives a principled criterion for surrogate screening and indicates the potential efficiency gain. We further develop a weighted bootstrap procedure for simultaneous confidence corridors (SCCs). As surrogate informativeness increases, SCC widths approach those obtained under complete observation, improving localization of significant effects that cannot be identified from the observed data alone. Simulations confirm accuracy and robustness under surrogate misspecification and with surrogates generated by image-to-image neural networks. Applied to spatially normalized PET images from ADNI, SSFR yields interpretable coefficient maps and uniformly narrower SCCs than an analysis using observed PET alone, enlarging the region over which age-related metabolic decline is simultaneously significant.
item.dc:creator: Guannan Wang, Yang Long, Shan Yu, Zhiling Gu, Lily Wang

item.title: The Science and Mythology of Sports Rankings: Evaluating the methods, assumptions, and attributes used to rank NCAA teams
item.description: arXiv:2611.27886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Selecting a sports-ranking system is not a purely mathematical decision. It also requires agreement about what the ranking should mean and what institutional purpose it should serve. This paper distinguishes four related but different tasks in sports ranking: prediction, retrospective evaluation, championship selection, and seeding; compares the governing philosophies of major ranking families; and identifies recurring errors in ranking debates. A descriptive comparison of nine NCAA Division I sport settings illustrates how schedule density, scoring environment, cross-conference connectivity, head-to-head meetings, and common-opponent availability vary from sport to sport. The central premise is that no ranking methodology is value-free. Every system reflects choices about evidence, competitive merit, and which tradeoffs are acceptable. The paper therefore offers a structured, multi-objective framework for evaluating ranking systems according to their intended purpose/goal rather than naming one universally superior method. Its principal contribution is to make the philosophical and institutional assumptions behind ranking decisions explicit, comparable, and testable.
item.dc:creator: Lawrence Feldman

item.title: Multi-scale dynamic latent space models improve inference for a social predator
item.description: arXiv:2611.27893v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Social networks are dynamic in nature. Examining changes in dynamic networks provides insights into the drivers and consequences of social interactions. Dynamic latent space models (DLSMs) quantify social tie strength through a distance measure between latent positions in an unobservable, low-dimensional space. Conditional on the latent positions, ties are assumed independent, and temporal dynamics are introduced through autocorrelated trajectories. These trajectories are typically modeled as random walks; however, random walks lack the mechanism to characterize network clustering, where individuals from the same group tend to form stronger ties than those across groups. Therefore, we extend the framework of DLSM to distinguish within-group dynamics from between-group dynamics. Our approach employs coupled movement models operating at two scales in the latent space to encode community structure using autoregressive processes with attraction. Through simulation studies, we show that when cluster separation is high, our framework improves coverage of linear predictors and enhances overall model fit relative to a naive DLSM. When cluster separation is moderate, performance remains comparable to that of the naive approach. In addition, our method demonstrates empirical computational advantages over the naive DLSM, with potential for further efficiency gains. We apply our framework to a case study of gray wolf (Canis lupus) interactions over three decades in Yellowstone National Park, where it provides improved model performance and novel insights into wolf social dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Xinyi Lu, T. J. Clark-Wolf, Matthew C. Metz

item.title: MSRyzen: An Agentic Platform for Unified Proteomics Analysis and Evidence-Centric Visualization
item.description: arXiv:2611.27246v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics is essential for comprehensive protein characterization, yet it relies on multistep computational workflows that typically demand tedious manual parameter tuning and complex software integration. Here, we present MSRyzen, an agent-driven framework that provides automated parameter optimization and extensible tool integration across bottom-up and top-down proteomics workflows. MSRyzen translates natural-language prompts into directed acyclic workflow graphs, optimizes analytical parameters guided by quantitative metrics and user-defined objectives, and incorporates new third-party software through standardized callable interfaces. Across four public top-down datasets, automated parameter optimization increased proteoform identifications by 3.6% to 15.8% compared to default settings at a 1% false discovery rate. To ensure transparent data interpretation, an interactive visualization interface coordinates identification metrics with peak-level spectral evidence and sequence coverage. Integrating adaptive tuning with multi-tiered spectral inspection, MSRyzen delivers an end-to-end, fully automated framework, dramatically reducing the operational barrier to modern mass spectrometry data analysis.
item.dc:creator: Yucheng Liao, Jubao Cheng, Zexu Xiao, Tao Yi, Jiaxiang Ding, Weijie Zhang

item.title: Combining Past Experimental Data for Efficient Estimation: A Shrinkage Approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.27655v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Firms routinely conduct randomized experiments, creating archives that could improve treatment-effect estimation in new experiments. However, past experiments evaluate related but different interventions, so their estimates may be biased for the current target. We study when and how borrowing from multiple auxiliary experiments can reduce the mean squared error (MSE) of a single treatment-effect estimate. In the oracle case, when biases and variances are known, borrowing from even one biased experiment strictly reduces MSE. In practice, we propose three shrinkage estimators and characterize their asymptotic MSE as the number of auxiliary experiments grows. Our analysis shows that average auxiliary bias and cross-study bias dispersion affect the relative performance of these estimators. As expected, smaller average bias magnitude generally improves performance. Surprisingly, bias dispersion can both benefit and harm our first estimator, the general plug-in estimator. On one hand, a more dispersed bias allows flexibility in cancelling the bias. On the other hand, the bias cancellation is imperfect as we only have an estimate of the bias, leading to overfitting. Motivated by this tradeoff, we propose a pooled plug-in estimator that restricts study-specific reweighting to limit this overfitting. However, both plug-in estimators can perform poorly when average bias is large. To address this, we develop a fixed-weight estimator with a hypothesis-testing gate that borrows only when the aggregate auxiliary mean is not significantly different from the target mean. Simulations illustrate the relative strengths of these estimators across bias environments and the relevance of the limiting analysis for finite collections of experiments. We also provide managerial guidance on which shrinkage estimator to use based on average bias and bias dispersion.
item.dc:creator: Qianxi Zhang, Dae Woong Ham, Stefanus Jasin

item.title: Extreme Value Inference with Measurement Error: Application to Earthquake Magnitudes
item.description: arXiv:2611.27897v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Extreme value analyses typically assume that observations are measured without error, yet many environmental measurements are subject to different levels of observational uncertainty depending on the context. Ignoring such measurement error can distort inference on the tail behaviour. In this paper, we focus on peaks-over-threshold models, where exceedances above a high threshold are typically modelled using the generalised Pareto distribution (GPD). We develop a statistical framework for extreme value inference when observations are noisy measurements of an underlying true variable. Measurement error introduces a particular challenge in threshold-based extreme value analysis, as latent exceedances may be observed below the threshold, while latent non-exceedances may be observed above it. To address this problem, we represent the latent distribution using a hybrid body--tail specification, combining a flexible nonparametric body with a GPD tail. We develop a computationally efficient partially censored likelihood inference approach for data of this structure. The framework allows the measurement error scale and the GPD parameters to depend on covariates. Simulation studies demonstrate biases on the tail inference from ignoring measurement error and that our approach overcomes such impacts. The methodology is motivated by, and illustrated using, the catalogue of induced earthquake magnitudes from the Groningen, Netherlands, one of the largest gas fields in the world.
item.dc:creator: Wanchen Yue, Israel Martinez Hernandez, Jonathan A. Tawn, Ross Towe, Zak Varty

item.title: Explicational statistics: research for an AI age
item.description: arXiv:2611.27961v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI is dramatically changing the statistical research landscape. I argue that production of a distinct category of statistical knowledge, which I refer to as explicational statistics, is actually becoming more valuable as AI increasingly automates other parts of the research process. I define explicational statistics, contextualize it in terms of other forms of statistical knowledge, and explain why I think the rise of AI makes it more valuable. I demonstrate my framework by first developing a new dimension reduction method, Ambient Embedding Projection, that can simultaneously visualize the intrinsic geometry of a data manifold along with how that manifold is embedded into ambient space. I then use my new method to conceive of a new statistical property of a collection of manifolds, related to metric distortion, that in single-cell biology can capture the ensemble behavior of cell populations. I apply these ideas to single-nuclei RNA-seq data from the brains of mice from different behavioral conditions to reveal potential cellular mechanisms of chronic social defeat stress.
item.dc:creator: Sihai Dave Zhao

item.title: Trajectory-based cycle-level pedestrian crash prediction at intersections: A novel non-linear link function for block maxima led Bayesian GEV framework addressing heterogeneous traffic conditions
item.description: arXiv:2510.12963v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This study develops a cycle-level framework for estimating pedestrian crash risk at signalized intersections under heterogeneous, non-lane-based traffic. Existing approaches often assume linear relationships between covariates and parameters, oversimplifying the complex, non-monotonic interactions among motorized vehicles (MVs), non-motorized vehicles (NMVs), and pedestrians. To address this limitation, the framework introduces a non-linear link function within a Bayesian generalized extreme value (GEV) structure to capture how traffic effects vary. It applies extreme value theory through the block maxima approach using post-encroachment time as a surrogate safety measure, with each signal cycle serving as an analysis block. It also proposes a behaviour-normalized modified crash risk (MRC) metric to account for pedestrians' habitual risk-taking behaviour in Dhaka's mixed traffic. Seven hierarchical Bayesian models were estimated using Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulation and compared using the deviance information criterion. Models with a non-linear link function only in the GEV location parameter fit the data better than their linear counterparts. Results suggest pedestrian speed is negatively associated with crash risk, while flow and speed of MVs, pedestrian flow, and NMV conflicting speed show positive associations, though all remain uncertain. The selected model's MRC estimate was close to the observed crashes at a 93% confidence level tuned to this dataset. These results suggest that the non-linear structure adds flexibility for capturing the non-stationary and non-linear nature of traffic extremes. This framework is a step towards proactive identification of pedestrian crash risk and after wider validation, it could support adaptive signal control and safety interventions in mixed-traffic environments.
item.dc:creator: Parvez Anowar, Nazmul Haque, Md Asif Raihan, Md Hadiuzzaman

item.title: A Deep Zero-Inflated Model of North Atlantic Right Whale Presence To Support Blue Economy Management
item.description: arXiv:2606.14403v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Effective modeling of endangered marine mammal species, such as the North Atlantic Right Whale, is critical for balancing marine conservation with the growing blue economy. Passive acoustic monitoring data collected by autonomous underwater vehicles provide new opportunities for localized marine species detection and oceanographic sensing, but introduce complex statistical challenges such as zero inflation, imperfect detection, and intricate dependence structures. In response, we propose the Deep Zero-Inflated Bernoulli (DeepZIB) model, a deep statistical method which jointly models latent species presence and conditional detection probabilities while learning complex habitat relationships from heterogeneous covariate information. We establish theoretical results on the model's structural properties and conduct simulation experiments to demonstrate its ability to recover underlying parameters and latent presence fields. Application to real-world passive acoustic monitoring data on the North Atlantic Right Whale along the U.S. East Coast demonstrates improved model adequacy and predictive performance in capturing the species' dynamic and spatially varying habitat. We demonstrate DeepZIB's ability to generate high-resolution, spatially and temporally varying presence maps, providing valuable insights for targeted and risk-aware management of blue economy industries, ranging from offshore and marine energy, to fisheries management and maritime transport
item.dc:creator: Jiaxiang Ji, Laura Nazzaro, Ahmed Aziz Ezzat

item.title: Towards Fair Comparisons of AI- and Physics-Based Weather Models for Extreme Events via the Weighted Potential CRPS
item.description: arXiv:2606.21170v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study whether deterministic AI weather prediction (AIWP) models issue more informative forecasts for extreme weather events than deterministic numerical weather prediction (NWP) models. The deterministic model output is subjected to statistical post-processing via isotonic distributional regression (IDR), or EasyUQ, before the resulting probabilistic forecasts are assessed using weighted versions of the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS). This extends the recently proposed Potential CRPS (PCRPS) measure to focus on extreme outcomes. Since IDR exhibits optimality properties with respect to weighted versions of the CRPS, the proposed approach inherits desirable properties of the PCRPS, and, in particular, facilitates fair comparisons between data-driven and physics-based models when forecasting extreme weather events. We apply this evaluation framework to forecasts in the WeatherBench 2 dataset issued by the AIWP models GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and FuXi, with the ECMWF's high-resolution NWP model serving as a physics-based reference. The forecast models are compared when predicting mean sea level pressure, temperature, wind speed, and precipitation extremes, defined as exceedances or non-exceedances of thresholds obtained from historical observation data. Across a range of extreme-event thresholds, including thresholds corresponding to record-breaking events, the ranking of the forecast models remains largely unchanged. We find that AIWP models, particularly GraphCast and FuXi, result in the most informative forecasts for extreme weather events across most settings, suggesting that AIWP models have the potential to outperform NWP models when forecasting extremes.
item.dc:creator: Tobias Biegert, Sam Allen, Annika Alber, Sebastian Lerch

item.title: Forecast combination under temporal constraints: An application to day-ahead electricity prices
item.description: arXiv:2607.22310v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Day-ahead electricity prices are forecast by many competing models and at several temporal granularities, from hourly prices to block and baseload products. The resulting forecasts suffer from two distinct problems: forecasts produced at different granularities are incoherent, as the aggregates do not match the averages of their components, and no single model is the most accurate in every market, period and level. We address both problems in one step by applying the coherent forecast combination framework, recently proposed for linearly constrained multiple time series, to temporal hierarchies. The resulting temporal coherent combination pools the forecasts that the competing experts produce at all the levels of the hierarchy into a single forecast that satisfies the aggregation constraints and has minimum error variance among the linear unbiased combinations. Since the optimal solution depends on a high-dimensional error covariance matrix, we compare different estimators obtained by crossing correlation structures with linear and nonlinear shrinkage approaches, and we contrast the simultaneous solution with sequential strategies. Using the base forecasts of four model classes for the German and Spanish day-ahead markets, the combined forecasts significantly outperform the base forecasts at every temporal level and are never significantly less accurate than the best reconciled expert, often improving upon it significantly.
item.dc:creator: Daniele Girolimetto

item.title: A Bayesian Distance-Weighted Ising Model for Task-Related Regional Analysis of Neuroimaging Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.25656v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neuroimaging analysis commonly involves identifying task-relevant brain regions and examining functional connectivity. These objectives are typically addressed separately, without a model-based framework. We propose a Bayesian distance-weighted Ising model that jointly quantifies regional importance for task-label prediction and functional connectivity between brain regions. The Ising model favors agreement between interacting labels. We extend it with region-specific interaction parameters and weights based on distances between functional signals. The parameters quantify regional importance for distinguishing tasks, while the weights measure functional connectivity through signal similarity between regions. Inference for this model is challenging because the signals may be observed on unequal time grids and the likelihood function contains an intractable normalizing constant. To address this, we use a basis expansion and an auxiliary variable Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm. We apply the method to functional near-infrared spectroscopy data from younger and older adults, comparing resting-state and task-related activity. The model reveals age-dependent patterns of regional importance and connectivity. Among younger adults, the left orbitofrontal cortex contributes more strongly to task discrimination than the dorsolateral prefrontal and frontopolar cortices, whereas regional differences are less evident among older adults. Older adults also exhibit greater bilateral connectivity between corresponding regions, consistent with reduced hemispheric lateralization.
item.dc:creator: Heesang Lee, Jongrak Park, Seoyoung Choi, Bokgyeong Kang, Nial Friel, Sanghoon Han, Jaewoo Park

item.title: Efficient and Debiased Learning of Average Hazard Under Non-Proportional Hazards
item.description: arXiv:2602.13475v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The hazard ratio from the Cox proportional hazards model is a ubiquitous summary of treatment effect. However, when hazards are non-proportional, the hazard ratio can lose a stable causal interpretation and become study-dependent because it effectively averages time-varying effects with weights determined by follow-up and censoring. We consider the average hazard (AH) as an alternative causal estimand: a population-level person-time event rate that remains well-defined and interpretable without assuming proportional hazards. Although AH can be estimated nonparametrically and regression-style adjustments have been proposed, existing approaches do not provide a general framework for flexible, high-dimensional nuisance estimation with valid sqrt{n} inference. We address this gap by developing a semiparametric, doubly robust framework for covariate-adjusted AH. We establish pathwise differentiability of AH in the nonparametric model, derive its efficient influence function, and construct cross-fitted, debiased estimators that leverage machine learning for nuisance estimation while retaining asymptotically normal, sqrt{n}-consistent inference under mild product-rate conditions. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed estimator achieves small bias and near-nominal confidence-interval coverage across proportional and non-proportional hazards settings, including crossing-hazards regimes where Cox-based summaries can be unstable. We illustrate practical utility in comparative effectiveness research by comparing immunotherapy regimens for advanced melanoma using SEER-Medicare linked data.
item.dc:creator: Xiang Meng, Lu Tian, Kenneth Kehl, Hajime Uno
